items.title: The Thanksgiving Table Bill: What Food Prices Mean for This Year's Holiday Dinner
items.body:
Every November, hosts face the same math problem: how much will it cost to feed everyone at the table? This year, many are doing that math while grocery prices remain stubbornly higher than they were a few years ago. Inflation has cooled from its peak, but cooling is not the same as falling. Most food prices have settled at a higher level, and shoppers still feel it at the register.

This guide explains where the money tends to go, why some items cost more than others, and how to trim the bill without sacrificing the meal. Figures for any given store or region will vary, so treat this as a framework for planning rather than a price quote.

## Where the Money Goes

A traditional Thanksgiving dinner is built from a handful of categories. Some of them make up most of the total.

- **The main course.** Turkey is usually the single biggest line item, especially for large gatherings. Prices depend on size, brand, and whether the bird is fresh, frozen, organic, or pasture-raised.
- **Dairy and baking staples.** Butter, cream, eggs, and milk show up in nearly every side dish and dessert. Butter and eggs in particular have been known to swing sharply in price.
- **Produce.** Potatoes, sweet potatoes, green beans, cranberries, onions, and celery are individually inexpensive, but they add up when you cook for a crowd.
- **Pantry basics.** Flour, sugar, stuffing mix, canned pumpkin, broth, and spices are easy to overlook until you are standing in the aisle with a full cart.
- **Beverages and extras.** Rolls, drinks, and appetizers can quietly push the total higher than expected.

## Why Turkey Prices Can Jump

Turkey costs are shaped by factors that sit far upstream of the grocery store. Animal disease outbreaks can shrink flocks and tighten supply. Feed costs, labor, and processing expenses all feed into the wholesale price. Retailers also use turkeys as a "loss leader" in the weeks before the holiday, discounting them to draw shoppers into the store and making up the difference on other items. That is why the price per pound can vary widely from one store to the next, even in the same town.

## How Tariffs and Fuel Costs Reach the Checkout Line

Prices on the shelf include more than the cost of the food itself. They reflect the cost of getting that food to you.

**Tariffs.** Many pantry items are imported, including some spices, coffee, cocoa, certain fruits and vegetables, and canned goods. When import taxes rise, importers and retailers often pass at least part of the cost along to shoppers. The effect is usually gradual and uneven. A tariff on one product category may show up as a small increase on dozens of items, rather than one dramatic price jump.

**Fuel and transportation.** Food travels by truck, rail, ship, and plane. When diesel and fuel prices rise, shipping gets more expensive, and that cost is built into the price of everything from fresh produce to frozen goods. Refrigerated transport is especially energy-intensive, which is one reason perishable items can feel the pinch more than shelf-stable ones.

**Labor, packaging, and energy.** Farms, processing plants, and stores all face higher operating costs. Packaging materials and electricity for refrigeration are part of that picture. These expenses rarely make headlines, but they help explain why prices do not fall quickly even when some commodity costs ease.

## Practical Ways to Trim the Bill

You do not need to give up the traditional meal to spend less. A few planning habits can make a real difference.

1. **Start with a headcount and a menu.** Decide how many people are coming and write down every dish before you shop. Over-buying is one of the most common sources of waste at holiday meals.
2. **Plan portions realistically.** A common rule of thumb is about one to one and a half pounds of turkey per person for a bone-in bird, which leaves some for leftovers. Buying a much larger bird than you need adds cost and waste.
3. **Compare store flyers and apps.** Stores often discount turkey, canned goods, and baking items in the weeks leading up to the holiday. Checking several flyers and loyalty programs can reveal meaningful differences.
4. **Buy shelf-stable items early.** Canned pumpkin, broth, flour, and sugar can be picked up over several weeks as they go on sale, spreading out the cost.
5. **Consider store brands.** For basics such as flour, sugar, canned vegetables, and broth, store brands are often comparable in quality and cheaper than name brands.
6. **Choose frozen or in-season produce.** Frozen green beans and other vegetables can be cheaper than fresh and just as nutritious. Seasonal items like squash, potatoes, and cranberries tend to be better values in the fall.
7. **Make some dishes from scratch.** Homemade cranberry sauce, stuffing, and rolls often cost less than store-bought versions, though your time is part of the trade-off.
8. **Share the load.** A potluck-style dinner, where guests each bring a dish, spreads the cost and the workload. Be clear about who is bringing what to avoid duplicates.
9. **Plan for leftovers.** Turkey sandwiches, soup, and casseroles stretch the value of the bird. Freeze extras before they spoil.
10. **Simplify the menu.** Two or three sides done well can be more satisfying than eight done halfway. Cutting a dish or two is often the easiest way to save.

## A Realistic Budget Mindset

It helps to set a target before you shop and track your spending as you go. Many shoppers find that a written list, a firm budget, and a willingness to swap ingredients when prices are high keep the total under control. If the turkey is pricey, a smaller bird or a turkey breast may be enough. If fresh items are expensive, frozen or canned versions can fill the gap.

It is also worth remembering what the holiday is about. A meal does not need to be elaborate to be memorable. Hosts who focus on the company and a few well-made dishes often find that the day goes just as well, and the bill is easier to swallow.

## The Bottom Line

Grocery prices remain a concern for many households, and the cost of a holiday dinner reflects everything from farm conditions to trade policy to the price of diesel. You cannot control those forces, but you can control how you plan, shop, and cook. With a clear menu, a bit of comparison shopping, and smart use of leftovers, you can put a satisfying Thanksgiving meal on the table without letting the bill take over the day.

*This article is for general informational purposes only and is not financial advice. Prices vary by store and region, so check current local prices when planning your purchases.*

items.title: Shoppers Slow Down: What a 0.2% October Retail Sales Gain Says About the Holiday Season
items.body:
After a strong September, American shoppers eased off the gas in October. Retail sales rose 0.2% for the month, according to the Census Bureau's advance estimate, following a 0.8% jump in September. The October figure matched what forecasters had expected, so it was not a surprise. It still gives us a useful chance to look at how consumers are behaving heading into the busiest shopping stretch of the year.

This article explains how to read the report, why fuel prices can squeeze other spending, and what the numbers may and may not tell us about the holidays. It is general information, not financial advice.

## The numbers in context

Retail sales measure the dollar value of purchases at stores, restaurants, online retailers, gas stations and other businesses. The monthly report is one of the most closely watched indicators of consumer demand. Consumer spending makes up roughly two-thirds of U.S. economic activity, so shifts in shopping habits matter well beyond store aisles.

A 0.8% gain followed by a 0.2% gain does not mean consumers have stopped spending. Sales are still growing. The pace has simply cooled from an unusually strong month. Economists often expect some "give-back" after a big jump, because a surge in one month can pull forward purchases that would otherwise have happened later.

## How to read a Census Bureau retail report

A single headline number hides a lot. A few habits help when you read the release.

**1. Check whether the figures are adjusted.** The headline number is usually seasonally adjusted, which smooths out predictable patterns such as holiday spikes and summer travel. That makes month-to-month comparisons fairer. Unadjusted figures show the raw totals.

**2. Remember that prices are not removed.** Retail sales are reported in nominal dollars. If prices rise 0.3% in a month, sales can grow 0.2% while the actual quantity of goods bought falls slightly. Comparing the sales figure with inflation data gives a better picture of real demand.

**3. Expect revisions.** The first estimate is an "advance" reading based on a sample of businesses. It is often revised in later releases, sometimes meaningfully. A 0.2% reading could later be adjusted up or down, and the prior month's number can change too.

**4. Look beneath the top line.** The report breaks sales into categories, including motor vehicles, building materials, grocery stores, restaurants, clothing, electronics and online retail. Many analysts also look at a narrower measure that excludes autos and gasoline, since those two categories can swing sharply with prices and supply and may obscure underlying trends.

**5. Compare against expectations.** Markets and commentators react less to the raw figure than to how it compares with forecasts. A result in line with consensus, as in October, usually signals continuity rather than a turning point.

## Why gasoline can crowd out other spending

Gas stations count as retail sales, so higher pump prices can lift the headline number even when people are not buying more of anything. Households do not have unlimited budgets, though. When a bigger share of income goes to fuel, there is less left for discretionary items like clothing, electronics, dining out and gifts.

That effect works in two directions:

- **Headline versus underlying strength.** A rise in fuel prices can make total sales look healthier than the rest of the economy actually is. Falling fuel prices can do the opposite, dragging down the total while leaving more money in household budgets for other purchases.
- **Squeezed budgets.** Gas is a necessity for most commuters. When it costs more, many families cut elsewhere, often on non-essential categories first. Lower-income households, which spend a larger share of income on fuel and other basics, tend to feel this most.

This is why economists look at the "control group" and ex-gasoline measures as well as the total. They help separate real changes in shopping behavior from price movements in a single category.

## What it could mean for holiday sales

It is tempting to treat one month of data as a forecast for November and December. That would overreach. Still, a few points are reasonable.

**Steady, not spectacular.** A modest gain suggests consumers are still spending but are more selective. Retailers may see a season that grows at a moderate pace rather than one driven by a rush of impulse buying.

**Promotions matter.** When shoppers are cautious, discounts and early sales events tend to carry more weight. Many retailers already start holiday promotions in October, which may pull some demand forward and affect how monthly numbers look.

**Online keeps gaining share.** Over the long run, e-commerce has taken a growing portion of retail spending. Holiday results for physical stores and online sellers often diverge, so category detail is worth watching.

**The big drivers are still ahead.** Employment, wage growth, borrowing costs and consumer confidence will shape the rest of the season. So will weather, shipping capacity and the timing of major sales days. No single data point settles the outcome.

## Practical takeaways for shoppers

If you are planning your own holiday budget, the broader story is less important than your own finances. A few simple steps can help:

- Set a total spending limit before shopping starts, and divide it among gifts, travel and food.
- Compare prices across several retailers, and check return policies.
- Be wary of "limited time" pressure. A real bargain will usually still be a bargain tomorrow.
- Try to avoid putting purchases on credit cards you cannot pay off promptly, since interest can erase any savings from a sale.

## The bottom line

October's 0.2% increase shows a consumer who is still spending but at a calmer pace after September's burst. Because the result matched expectations, it is best read as a sign of continuity. For the holidays, the more useful questions are how much of the gain came from price changes rather than real purchases, how households are handling fuel and other living costs, and what the next reports show. Revisions and new data in the coming weeks will provide a clearer picture.

*This article is for general informational purposes only and does not constitute financial, investment or professional advice. Figures cited are based on the advance estimate and may be revised.*

items.title: Energy Pushes Inflation Higher: Inside October's 0.4% Jump in Consumer Prices
items.body:
Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, a faster pace than most forecasters expected, while core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, held at 0.3%. The gap between those two numbers points to the main driver of the month: energy.

This article explains what the headline and core figures mean, which categories fed the increase, and why one strong monthly reading doesn't settle the debate over where inflation is heading.

## The Numbers at a Glance

- **Headline consumer prices:** up 0.4% for the month, above forecasts.
- **Core prices (excluding food and energy):** up 0.3%, unchanged from the prior pace.
- **The difference:** roughly 0.1 percentage point, which is attributable mostly to more volatile categories such as energy.

A 0.4% monthly gain looks modest, but economists often look at what it implies over a year. If a 0.4% pace held for twelve months, it would compound to close to 5% annual inflation. That is well above the 2% target the Federal Reserve has set. A 0.3% pace compounds to a little under 4%. That is why even small monthly differences get close attention.

## Why Energy Mattered So Much

Energy prices are among the most volatile parts of the consumer price index. Gasoline, electricity, and natural gas can all move sharply from month to month because of weather, refinery activity, seasonal demand, and global supply conditions.

Energy has an outsized effect on headline readings for three reasons:

1. **It is bought often.** Households fill up their tanks and pay utility bills every month, so changes are felt quickly.
2. **It is volatile.** A swing of several percent in a single month is not unusual, which can move the overall index even when other prices are steady.
3. **It feeds into other costs.** Higher fuel and power costs can eventually show up in transportation, shipping, and food prices.

Because the headline index includes energy and the core index does not, an energy-led month tends to lift the first number while leaving the second largely unchanged. That is the pattern seen in October.

## Other Categories in the Mix

Energy was not the only contributor. Several other areas typically shape the monthly reading:

- **Shelter.** Rent and housing-related costs make up the largest single share of the index. They move slowly, but they rarely fall quickly, so they often hold core inflation up.
- **Food.** Grocery and restaurant prices can add or subtract a few hundredths of a percentage point depending on the month.
- **Services.** Items such as medical care, insurance, and transportation services have been persistent sources of upward pressure in recent years.
- **Goods.** Prices for many manufactured goods have been flatter, which helps offset some of the pressure from services.

A core reading of 0.3% suggests that underlying price growth remains steady rather than accelerating. It also shows that it hasn't cooled as much as policymakers might prefer.

## Why One Hot Month Doesn't Settle the Debate

It is tempting to treat each monthly report as a verdict. Economists are generally more careful, for several reasons.

**Monthly data is noisy.** Seasonal adjustments, weather events, and temporary supply disruptions can all distort a single month. A figure that looks high may be partly reversed the next month.

**Energy can reverse.** If the increase came from a short-term spike in fuel or utility costs, prices may ease later. The effect on headline inflation would then fade.

**Core is the steadier guide.** Because core inflation strips out the most volatile items, many analysts consider it a better signal of where prices are going over the next several months. A steady 0.3% is neither a clear sign of re-acceleration nor of a sustained cooling.

**Trends matter more than points.** Analysts often look at three-month and six-month averages, as well as year-over-year changes, to see through temporary swings. One reading above forecasts does not establish a new trend, just as one below forecasts would not have ended the debate.

**Revisions and surveys can change the picture.** Government statistical agencies sometimes revise earlier figures, and surveys of consumers and businesses offer additional context about price expectations.

## What It Means for Households

For most households, the practical effect of an energy-led increase shows up at the gas pump and on utility bills. Those costs are hard to avoid, so they can feel larger than the headline number suggests. Higher energy costs may also leave less room in budgets for other spending.

Some general points to keep in mind:

- Track your own spending categories rather than relying only on national averages. Your personal inflation rate depends on what you buy.
- Seasonal changes in heating and cooling costs can be planned for ahead of time.
- Short-term price moves in energy often don't last, so large financial decisions made on one month's data carry more risk.

## What to Watch Next

Several indicators will help show whether October was a one-off or part of a broader pattern:

- **Next month's CPI report**, especially the core figure and the energy component.
- **Wholesale and producer prices**, which can signal pressure that has not yet reached consumers.
- **Wage growth**, since rising pay can sustain demand for services.
- **Central bank communications**, which show how policymakers read the data and whether they see risks to their inflation goal.

## The Bottom Line

October's 0.4% increase was a firmer reading than expected, and energy did much of the work. With core inflation steady at 0.3%, the report points to ongoing but not accelerating underlying price pressure. A single month is a data point, not a trend, and the inflation debate will turn on whether the coming months confirm or reverse what October showed.

*This article is for general informational purposes only and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Figures are rounded and based on the reported monthly changes; refer to official government statistical releases for complete data.*

items.title: [Consumer Psychology #11] Why $19.99 Feels Cheaper Than $20: The Psychology of Price
items.body:
> A price is never judged alone. We compare it to a number in our heads, read it from left to right, and react to how a discount is framed, so the same dollar amount can feel like a bargain or a rip-off.

## Today's Concept

Economics textbooks often treat price as a simple fact: a product costs $20, and you decide whether it is worth $20 to you. Real shoppers don't work that way. Consumer psychology shows that people judge prices **relative to something else**, and that small details in how a price is shown can change how it feels. Three ideas explain most of this.

**1. Reference price: "Compared to what?"**
A reference price is the benchmark you use to decide whether a price is high or low. It comes from two places:

- **Internal reference price** is the number already in your memory: what you paid last time, what you think is "normal," what a friend said they paid.
- **External reference price** is a number the seller shows you: a "Was $80" tag, a manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP), or a pricier item placed right next to the one being sold.

A $60 jacket feels like a deal if you expected $90, and feels expensive if you expected $40. The price itself didn't change. The comparison did. This connects to *anchoring*, the tendency for the first number we see to pull later judgments toward it.

**2. Prices ending in 9: the left-digit effect**
Why do so many prices end in .99 or 9? One well-supported explanation is the **left-digit effect**. We read numbers left to right, and the first digit gets more attention than the rest. So $19.99 tends to register as "nineteen-something," not "basically twenty," even though the difference is a single cent. Research has found the effect is strongest when the leftmost digit changes ($2.99 vs. $3.00), not when it stays the same ($2.89 vs. $2.90).

Prices ending in 9 also carry a second signal: many shoppers have learned to associate them with sales and discounts. In one well-known field experiment with a women's clothing catalog, the same dress sold more at $39 than at either $34 or $44. The 9-ending outsold even a *lower* price. That said, 9-endings are not magic. Luxury and premium brands often prefer round numbers ($200, not $199.99) precisely because round prices signal quality rather than bargain.

**3. Discount perception: framing the savings**
The same discount can be described in different ways, and the description matters.

- **Percent vs. dollars:** For cheaper items, a percentage often looks bigger ("25% off" a $12 item sounds better than "$3 off"). For expensive items, the dollar figure often looks bigger ("$300 off" a $1,500 laptop sounds better than "20% off"). Marketers sometimes call this the "rule of 100": below $100, show the percent; above $100, show the dollars. It's a useful rule of thumb, not a law.
- **Relative savings:** People will drive across town to save $10 on a $30 item but often won't for $10 off a $1,000 item, even though the savings are identical. We tend to judge savings as a proportion of the price, not in absolute dollars.

## In Everyday Life

A famous U.S. retail story shows how strong reference prices are. In 2012, **JCPenney** tried to simplify its pricing. Instead of marking items up and then running constant sales and coupons, it moved to "fair and square" everyday prices that were often similar to what shoppers had been paying after discounts anyway.

On paper, customers weren't losing money. But they lost the "Was $50, now $29.99" comparison, and with it the feeling of winning a deal. Sales fell sharply, the CEO behind the change was replaced in 2013, and the company brought back its sales and coupons.

You can see the same psychology on any weekend at Target, Walmart, or on Amazon: a crossed-out "List Price," a "Save 30%" badge, or a $29.99 tag sitting next to a $49.99 "premium" version. Each one is designed to give you a reference point that makes the price in front of you look reasonable.

## 3-Line Summary

1. We judge prices against a **reference price**, either remembered (internal) or shown by the seller (external), so context can make the same price feel cheap or expensive.
2. Prices ending in 9 work partly because of the **left-digit effect** and partly because shoppers link them with sales; round prices tend to signal quality instead.
3. How a **discount** is framed (percent vs. dollars, relative vs. absolute savings) changes how big it feels, even when the money saved is the same.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1.** A "Was $120" tag printed next to a $79 price is an example of:
- (a) Internal reference price
- (b) External reference price
- (c) The left-digit effect

**Q2.** O/X: The left-digit effect predicts that changing a price from $4.00 to $3.99 will typically feel like a bigger drop than changing it from $4.50 to $4.49.

**Q3.** A store is discounting a $1,200 sofa by 15%. Based on the "rule of 100," which framing is likely to look more attractive?
- (a) "15% off"
- (b) "$180 off"
- (c) They will feel exactly the same

## 📚 Key Terms

- **Reference price:** The benchmark a shopper uses to decide whether a price is high, low, or fair.
- **Internal reference price:** A benchmark stored in memory, based on past purchases, expectations, or what feels "normal."
- **External reference price:** A benchmark supplied at the point of sale, such as a "Was" price, MSRP, or a nearby comparison product.
- **Left-digit effect:** The tendency to focus on a price's first digit, so $2.99 feels noticeably cheaper than $3.00.
- **Anchoring:** The tendency for an initial number to pull later judgments toward it.

---

*Answers: Q1 (b). The seller is supplying the comparison point, so it's an external reference price; an internal one would come from your own memory. Q2 O. Going from $4.00 to $3.99 changes the leftmost digit (4 → 3), which is where the effect is strongest; $4.50 to $4.49 keeps the leftmost digit the same. Q3 (b). For items above roughly $100, the dollar amount ($180) is usually a bigger, more impressive-looking number than the percentage (15%), even though they describe the same discount.*
